newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen takes aim at monarchists.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen takes aim at monarchists.

text.p: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen has taken aim at those threatening his grip on power: King Norodom Sihanouk, the royalist FUNCINPEC party and others linked to the monarchy.

Hun Sen, who runs the Cambodian government in uneasy partnership with Sihanouk's son, Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, fears that the pro-monarchist cause may triumph in local and national elections in 1997 and 1998.

Of particular concern to Hun Sen and his backers is the possibility that the 74-year-old Sihanouk may abdicate and use his enormous popularity to propel FUNCINPEC and its allies to victory in the polls, analysts said on Wednesday.
With this in mind, Hun Sen said last week that the royal family should be barred from politics, adding that the elections would be cancelled if the king joined the political fray.
Messages of support for Hun Sen's position have been aired over radio stations loyal to his powerful Cambodian People's Party (CPP).
Sihanouk said last month he was seriously thinking of abdicating, but pledged not to run in the elections or form a party for the polls.
That will come as cold comfort to Hun Sen, aware of the king's grass roots popularity and of his 1955 abdication to lead a political front that kept him in power as a simple prince until a 1970 coup.
Sihanouk was re-elected as a king who "reigns but does not rule," on the restoration of a constitutional monarchy in 1993.

"He knows that the king still has many supporters among the people, especially in the rural area," said FUNCINPEC member of parliament Ahmed Yahya. If the king became a politician, "Hun Sen feels the king is going to win the elections," he said.

"I think he's worried because he thinks the king still has enough clout," an Asian diplomat said, noting that FUNCINPEC had beaten the incumbent CPP in 1993 elections largely on the back of Sihanouk's popularity.
He said Hun Sen knew that his many welfare projects might not be enough to beat a party aligned with Sihanouk. "He doesn't want FUNCINPEC to use the king again as their symbol."
Hun Sen's fears about the strength of the royalist cause may be well-founded, some analysts say.
Ranariddh has said that while he does not want his father to abdicate, the royalists must naturally support him if he quits and enters politics.
The prince also said that any move to postpone elections was unconstitutional, and he stressed the royal family's rights to partake in politics as Cambodian citizens.

One Cambodian analyst described Hun Sen's warning to the royal family to stay out of politics as an attack on the institution of the monarchy, on FUNCINPEC and on the National United Front alliance set up by Ranariddh last month with pro-monarchists.
The alliance includes the popular opposition Khmer National Party (KNP) of ex-finance minister Sam Rainsy, who was expelled from FUNCINPEC over policy differences in 1995

Some analysts believe the CPP is preparing to strike at the KNP in a bid to further weaken the election chances of Hun Sen's rivals, noting that Sam Rainsy has been linked by the CPP to the murder last year of Hun Sen's brother-in-law.
They fear Sam Rainsy could be arrested.
The royalists are expected to map out their own strategy and response to the Hun Sen threat at a three-day congress that was opening on Wednesday.
